Watches of the Night
WOCH-iz uv thuh NYT
noun
From the Old English wæcce, “a waking, a keeping guard,” kin to wake and watch; a “watch” of the night is the span for which a sentinel stood his post. Hebrew reckoning knew three such divisions of the dark; the Roman, four.

Biblical Definition

A watch of the night is one of its appointed divisions — not the darkness itself, but a guarded portion of it, the span for which a sentinel stood his post before the next relieved him. The modern ear hears “night” as one unbroken block; the Scripture divides it. Israel of old kept three watches — hence Gideon came “in the beginning of the middle watch” (Jdg 7:19), and it was “in the morning watch” that the LORD looked through the pillar of fire and troubled the Egyptians (Exo 14:24). Jeremiah bids stricken Zion cry “in the beginning of the watches” (Lam 2:19). By our Lord’s day Rome had imposed four, and the Gospel names them in order: “at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning.” It was in the last of these that Christ came upon the water: “in the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea” (Mat 14:25) — the coldest watch, when the disciples had toiled all night and were spent, and He came. The watches are the believer’s hours of prayer: “When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches” (Psa 63:6). And they measure a mercy, for to the LORD who never sleeps a thousand years “are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night” (Psa 90:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

One of the divisions of the night during which a sentinel kept guard — three by Hebrew reckoning, four by Roman.

WATCH, a division of the night; the period during which a sentinel or guard is on duty.

From Old English wæcce, a waking, a keeping guard through the dark hours.

The Hebrews parted the night into three watches; the Romans into four.

Christ came to the labouring disciples in the fourth watch of the night (Mat 14:25).

The godly remember God and pour out prayer in the night watches (Psa 63:6).

Key Scripture

Lam 2:19 — "Arise, cry out in the night: in the beginning of the watches pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord: lift up thy hands toward him for the life of thy young children, that faint for hunger in the top of every street."

Psa 63:6 — "When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches."

Psa 90:4 — "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."

Mat 14:25 — "And in the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea."

Modern Corruption

Not a poetic synonym for “night,” but its ordered divisions; the word recovers the dark hours as a season of appointed watch and prayer.

expand to see more

The honest drift to name here is the flattening of the phrase. A modern reader, meeting “the night watches,” hears only a soft word for the dark and misses the ordered thing the Scripture means. A watch was a shift — a fixed span with a beginning and an end, when a man stood armed against whatever the night might bring, and was relieved by another when his turn was done. To lose the word is to lose the picture: the changing of the guard, the trumpet at the middle watch, the LORD looking down in the morning watch upon a drowning enemy. The night is not one undivided weight; it is measured, manned, and kept.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the night as a season of watch. The saint is not to sleep out the dark like the world, but to keep his post in it — to remember God upon his bed and meditate on Him in the night watches, to arise in the beginning of the watches and pour out his heart like water before the face of the Lord. The longest night has its divisions, and each has its duty; and over the whole of it stands the God to whom a thousand years are but a single watch. The believer keeps his watch because his Keeper never sleeps.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means one of the guarded divisions of the night, the span of a sentinel’s duty.

expand to see more

Watch — Old English wæcce, “a waking, a keeping guard.”

A watch of the night is the span for which a sentinel stood his post.

The Hebrews kept three watches; the Romans divided the night into four.

The four are named at even, midnight, cockcrowing, and morning (Mar 13:35).

Christ walked the sea in the fourth watch, and the LORD saw in the morning watch (Exo 14:24).

Usage

"Watches of the night are its divisions, not a mere word for the dark — each a shift with its own duty."

"Christ came in the fourth watch, when the rowers were spent: the darkest watch is not beyond His reach."

"David meditated in the night watches: the believer keeps his post while the world sleeps."
